div.head: II Atr 1.1
div.ab: ⁊ gif ænig sciphere on Englaland hergie, þæt we habban heora ealra fultum; ⁊ we him sculon mete findon, ða hwile ðe hy mid us beoð.
Si naualis exercitus Angliam infestet, ut habeamus omnium eorum auxilium; et ministrabimus eis uictum, quamdiu nobiscum erunt.
⁊ gif ænig sciphere on Englaland hergie, þæt we habban heora ealra fultum; ⁊ we him sculon mete findon, ða hwile ðe hy mid us beoð.

Und wenn irgend ein Schiffsheer England verheert: dass wir [gegen dies] aller jener [Nordleute] Hilfe erhalten; und wir sind verpflichtet, ihnen Proviant zu liefern, die Zeit, da sie bei uns sein werden.
And if any naval force harries England: that we have the help of all of them [the Northmen against it]; and we are obliged to supply them with provisions for as long as they are with us.
And if any hostile fleet harry in England, we shall have the help of all of them; and we shall be under the obligation of finding provisions for them, as long as they remain with us.
And that, if any fleet harry in England, we are to have the help of them all; and we must supply them with food as long as they are with us.

Zunächst, wenn nicht allein, ist ein Nordischer Angriff verstanden. Der Eine Vertragsschliesser verpflichtet also keineswegs, wie England, auch seine Landsleute in Skandinavien oder der Denalagu Britanniens
Primarily, if not exclusively, a Norse attack is meant. The one contracting party thus by no means binds, as England does, his fellow-countrymen in Scandinavia or in the Danelaw of Britain as well
Dieser Name wird statt Britannien oder Angelcynn erst kurz vorher herrschend; Miller Placenames in Bede 18; Freeman Norman conq. I 538
This name becomes predominant, in place of Britain or Angelcynn, only shortly before; Miller Placenames in Bede 18; Freeman Norman conq. I 538
Dass dieses Bündnis sich gegen Wales richte, dessen Fürst Meredydd damals England feindlich war, wie Hunt (in Dict. nat. biogr. s. v. Ethelred) meint, schliesst der Text deutlich aus
The text clearly rules out that this alliance was directed against Wales, whose prince Meredydd was then hostile to England, as Hunt (in Dict. nat. biogr. s. v. Ethelred) thinks

Steenstrup (Normannerne III 238) folgert wohl mit Recht, das Heer sollte nicht sofort abziehen. Die Verproviantierung ist dann also nicht oder nicht bloss für einen etwa künftigen Bündnisfall gemeint. So nahm 1012 Æthelred ‘45 Schiffe von dem Heere’ in Dienst zur Landesbewachung, gegen Lieferung von Proviant und Kleidung

Steenstrup (Normannerne III 238) probably rightly concludes that the army was not to depart immediately. The provisioning is therefore not meant, or not merely meant, for a possible future case of alliance. Thus in 1012 Æthelred took ‘45 ships from the army’ into his service to guard the country, in return for the supply of provisions and clothing
The form Englaland apparently came into use about this time replacing the earlier name Angelcynnes land (see Sax. Chr. ii. p. 375). This is its first appearance in the Laws.
Cf. for a similar arrangement Sax. Chr. ann. 1006 E, 1012 E.

The invading force probably wintered in England. The Battle of Maldon which preceded the treaty is ascribed to August 11th by an eleventh century calendar, quoted, with references, by Napier and Stevenson, Crawford Charters, p. 88. In Olafss. Tr. Chap. 33, there is a romantic story of Olaf’s marriage to an Irish princess while he was in England.
